Antisocial has two distinct meanings — one formal and serious, one casual and everyday. Both are in wide use, and knowing both will help you understand and use the word correctly in any context.
Meaning 1 — Against or harmful to society (the formal meaning)

Antisocial means acting in ways that harm, disturb, or work against the wellbeing of other people and society as a whole.

This isn't about being a little rude or awkward. Antisocial behavior, in this sense, actively goes against the basic rules and values that allow people to live together — things like respecting others' safety, property, and shared spaces.

Examples of antisocial behavior:

  • Vandalism (destroying public property)
  • Bullying or harassment
  • Deliberately intimidating neighbors
  • Loud, aggressive behavior in public that disturbs others
  • Theft and fraud

Notice that all of these have one thing in common: they damage other people or the community. The person isn't just minding their own business — they are crossing a line that hurts others.

This is the meaning used in law and public policy. Many countries have laws specifically targeting "antisocial behavior" — laws against things like noise disturbances, aggressive begging, gang intimidation, and so on.
Meaning 2 — Not wanting to socialize (the everyday, informal meaning)

In everyday conversation, people very commonly use antisocial to mean someone who avoids other people or doesn't like socializing.

You'll hear sentences like:

  • "He never comes to parties — he's so antisocial."
  • "Don't be antisocial, come sit with us!"
  • "She spent the whole trip alone in her room."

This usage is extremely widespread, especially in British English, and you will encounter it constantly. Using antisocial this way sounds perfectly natural in casual conversation.
An important precision: antisocial vs. unsociable

Strictly speaking, the "correct" word for someone who simply doesn't enjoy socializing is unsociable — meaning not fond of company, preferring to be alone.

Unsociable is neutral. An unsociable person just doesn't particularly want to hang out with people — there's no hostility, no harm.

Antisocial (in its precise sense) implies something stronger: going against society, not just away from it.

However, because antisocial is used so frequently in the casual sense (Meaning 2), the line between the two words has blurred in modern English. Both usages are understood and accepted. Just know that if you want to be maximally precise about someone who merely keeps to themselves, unsociable is the sharper choice.

You may occasionally see the word asocial (written with a single "a" at the start). This is different from antisocial.

  • Asocial = simply indifferent to social interaction; neither seeking it nor being hostile about it. Neutral.
  • Antisocial = actively working against social norms, or avoiding them in a way that is disruptive or harmful.

Think of it this way: an asocial person walks past people without caring to interact. An antisocial person (formal sense) pushes them aside.

In clinical psychology and psychiatry, antisocial has a very specific technical meaning, used in the diagnosis called Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD).

A person with ASPD shows a deep, long-term pattern of:

  • Disregarding the rights and feelings of others
  • Manipulating or deceiving people for personal gain
  • Impulsive, reckless behavior with no remorse
  • Repeatedly breaking social rules, laws, and norms

This is far more serious than just "not wanting to go to parties." When a psychologist uses the word antisocial, they mean this — a persistent disregard for others that often causes real harm.
Critical distinction: antisocial ≠ introverted or shy

This is one of the most common confusions, so it deserves special attention.

Introverted means you prefer quieter environments, feel drained by too much social activity, and recharge by spending time alone. Introverts still care about people and treat them well — they simply need less social stimulation. This is a personality trait, not a disorder, and it is completely normal.

Shy means you feel nervous or anxious in social situations. A shy person may want to connect with others but feels held back by anxiety. Again, this has nothing to do with hostility toward others.

Neither introversion nor shyness is antisocial. An antisocial person (formal meaning) isn't just quiet or nervous — they show active disregard or contempt for others' rights and feelings.

Antisocial behavior isn't all-or-nothing. It exists on a spectrum:

  • Mild: Ignoring basic social courtesies, being persistently rude, cutting in queues deliberately, playing loud music that disturbs neighbors.
  • Moderate: Bullying, harassment, intimidation, vandalism.
  • Severe: Violence, predatory manipulation, repeated criminal behavior.

The word antisocial can be applied across this range, though for very severe patterns it overlaps with clinical language (like ASPD).

Formal meaning: Antisocial describes behavior that actively harms, disrupts, or works against the wellbeing of other people and society — from vandalism and bullying to serious crime.

Informal meaning: Antisocial also commonly means someone who avoids people and doesn't like socializing — though unsociable is technically the more precise word for this.

In psychology: Antisocial refers to a persistent, clinical pattern of disregarding others' rights, lacking empathy, and repeatedly violating social norms (Antisocial Personality Disorder).

What it is not: Being introverted, shy, or simply quiet. Those are personality traits with no element of harm toward others.

The heart of the word is the prefix anti-, meaning "against" — so antisocial always carries some sense of being against the social world, whether mildly (avoiding it) or seriously (harming it).
